statement: For the uniform probability measure on [0,L], L>0, Var(X)=L^2/12, its optimal Euclidean Poincare constant is L^2/pi^2, and its Cheeger constant (outer Minkowski perimeter divided by min mass) is 2/L. Consequently no universal unnormalized Poincare upper bound or Cheeger lower bound holds for all log-concave probabilities under arbitrary dilation.
assumptions: uniform measure on a convex interval is log-concave
proof: Translate to [0,L]. The Neumann cosine expansion yields Var(f)<=L^2/pi^2 integral |f'|^2 and equality for cos(pi x/L). A half interval has perimeter 1/L and mass 1/2. Any nontrivial finite-perimeter subset of the interval has at least one interior endpoint, so its perimeter/min mass>=2/L. Var(X) follows by integration. Dilation sends the two constants to infinity and zero respectively.

statement: For every d>=2, whitening the uniform measure on Delta_d={x_i>=0,sum x_i<=1} gives an isotropic log-concave Y and an edge-parallel unit v. For T=<v,Y> and Z=Proj_(v-perp)Y, ess sup_Z C_P(T|Z)=2(d+1)(d+2)/pi^2, E_Z C_P(T|Z)=12/pi^2, and ess inf_Z h(T|Z)=sqrt(2/((d+1)(d+2))). On an event of probability (d+1)/2^d, C_P(T|Z)>=(d+1)(d+2)/(2 pi^2).
assumptions: Euclidean orthogonal conditioning in whitened coordinates
essential extrema relative to the projection marginal
proof: Cov(X)=(I-J/(d+1))/((d+1)(d+2)); inverse K(I+J). Let A=Cov(X)^(-1/2), a=sqrt(2K), v=Ae1/a. Orthogonal projection PA fixes X2,...,Xd since ker(PA)=span(e1). With S=sum_{j>=2} Xj, T=a(X1-(1-S)/2) conditional on Z is uniform on an interval of length a(1-S). S has density d(d-1)s^(d-2)(1-s). Apply exact uniform-interval constants, E(1-S)^2=6/K and P(S<=1/2)=(d+1)/2^d. Every small positive S interval has positive projection mass, so these are essential extrema rather than exceptional fibers.

statement: For the isotropic simplex and direction of claim 002, the least C with E Var(f(Y)|Z)<=C E|partial_v f(Y)|^2 for all locally Lipschitz f with finite energies is 2(d+1)(d+2)/pi^2. Thus replacing the weighted conditional constants by their arithmetic mean 12/pi^2 is false; the necessary-to-mean factor is exactly (d+1)(d+2)/6.
assumptions: construction and orthogonal conditioning of claim 002
finite full and directional gradient energy
test function may depend on both T and Z
proof: The fiber inequality yields the upper bound with ess sup C_P. For the lower bound use f=eta(S) sin(pi T/(a(1-S))), with eta nonzero smooth and supported in (epsilon/4,epsilon/2). Conditional mean is zero; conditional sine variance is 1/2 and directional energy is pi^2/(2a^2(1-S)^2). Since partial_v S=0, the Rayleigh quotient is at least a^2(1-epsilon)^2/pi^2. The support has positive mass and finite full gradient energy for every epsilon>0. Let epsilon go to zero.

statement: In the isotropic simplex construction of claim 002, for every integer k>=1 let t=1-S, f(Y)=T t^k and M_p=(p+1)!d!/(d+p)!. Then E[f|Z]=0, E Var(f|Z)=(K/6)M_(2k+2), E|partial_v f|^2=M_(2k), and E|grad f|^2=[1+k^2(d-1)/(3(d+1))]M_(2k). The directional quotient is (K/6)(2k+2)(2k+3)/[(d+2k+1)(d+2k+2)], and the full quotient divides this by the displayed transverse-energy factor.
assumptions: Whitening, scalar fiber variables and unit direction exactly as in claim 002
Full Euclidean gradient includes all transverse derivatives
proof: t has Beta(2,d-1) law, giving M_p by the integer beta integral. Conditional mean of T is zero and conditional variance is K t^2/6. For b=grad_Y S, b is orthogonal to v and |b|^2=2(d-1)/((d+1)K), by the covariance quadratic form. Thus grad f=v t^k-k T t^(k-1)b has vanishing cross term. Integrating its two squared terms gives the full multiplier 1+k^2(d-1)/(3(d+1)). All f are polynomials on a compact simplex, with finite energy.
